chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abī Naṣr al-Bazantī narrated from Muhammad ibn Samāʿah, from Zurārah, from Abū Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said:
I asked him about a man who said to his wife, 'You are forbidden to me.'

He said: "If I had authority over him, I would have struck his head and said to him: Allah, the Exalted, has made her lawful for you, so who made her forbidden to you? He has done nothing more than lie, claiming that what Allah has made lawful for him is forbidden. Neither divorce nor expiation takes effect upon him."
So I said to him: then what about the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic:

O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful. Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths.

So He made expiation binding upon him in it. He said: "He only forbade to himself his bondwoman Māriyah and swore that he would not approach her. The expiation was only imposed upon him for the oath, and it was not imposed upon him for the prohibition itself."

key_terms.تَحِلَّةَ: release or dissolution, here of oaths
key_terms.حَرَامٌ: declared forbidden or unlawful in speech
key_terms.سُلْطَانٌ: authority or power to discipline or judge
key_terms.كَفَّارَةٌ: expiation required for certain violations such as breaking an oath

ai.seo_question: Does saying to one’s wife 'you are forbidden to me' count as divorce or require expiation in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith states that a man saying to his wife, 'You are forbidden to me,' does not thereby effect divorce and does not incur kaffarah merely by that statement. It also explains the Quranic passage about the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم as relating to an oath, with expiation attached to the oath rather than to the act of declaring something forbidden.
